# Insights into Free Drug Release from Efficacious N-Acyl O-Aminophenol Duocarmycin Prodrugs

**Authors:** Nilanjana Chakraborty; Jelena Momirov; Aleksandar Radakovic; Shreyosree Chatterjee; Aaron M. Kirchhoff; Anna-Lena Kolb; Thomas J. West; Brittany B. Sanchez; Salvador Martinez-Bartolome; Anthony Saviola; Daniel McClatchy; John R. Yates; Jason S. Chen; Luke L. Lairson; Brunie H. Felding; Dale L. Boger

**Affiliations:** †Department of Chemistry and The Skaggs Institute for Chemical Biology, The Scripps Research Institute, 10550 N. Torrey Pines Road, La Jolla, California 92037, United States | ‡Department of Molecular Medicine, The Scripps Research Institute, 10550 N. Torrey Pines Road, La Jolla, California 92037, United States

## Abstract

Acyclic and cyclic N-acyl O-aminophenol prodrugs of duocarmycin analogues were reported as members of a unique class of reductively cleaved prodrugs that map seamlessly onto the duocarmycin family of natural products. Although these prodrugs were explored with the expectations that they may be cleaved selectively within hypoxic tumor environments that have intrinsically higher concentrations of reducing nucleophiles, the remarkable stability of some such prodrugs suggest another mechanism of free drug release is operative. The prototype of such chemically unreactive N-acyl O-aminophenol prodrugs is 1, which proved remarkably efficacious in vivo in vertebrate tumor models, was found to lack the toxicity characteristic of traditional chemotherapeutic drugs as well as the free drugs in the class (e.g., myelosuppression) and to display a preferential site (intracellular), slow and sustained rate, and potentially unique mechanism of free drug release. Herein, we detail studies that provide insights into this stereoselective mechanism of free drug release. Combined, the results of the studies are consistent with an exclusive protein-mediated (enantio)selective activation and free drug release from prodrug 1 by N–O bond cleavage preferentially in cancer cell lines versus cultured normal human cell lines effected by a cytosolic cysteine-based enzyme and suggest that the activating protein is one that is selectively expressed, upregulated, or preferentially activated in cancer cell lines potentially constituting a new oncology targeted precision therapy.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Duocarmycin SA1 is a widely recognized member of a class of natural products that also includes duocarmycin A,2 yatakemycin,3 and CC-10654 (Figure 1A), which exhibits exceptionally potent antitumor activity derived from an ability to alkylate DNA in a sequence selective manner.5–9 Extensive studies of the natural products, their synthetic unnatural enantiomers,10,11 and key analogues6 identified structural features that control DNA alkylation selectivity, rate, efficiency,12 and catalysis,13,14 defining the fundamental relationships between structure, reactivity, and biological activity.7 However, the exceptional potency and narrow therapeutic window of the natural products and their analogues have precluded clinical advancement.

The DNA alkylation is mediated by the activated cyclopropane in the alkylation subunit. A more controlled DNA alkylation is possible by converting the cyclopropane into an open chain derivative (seco-derivative) and masking the phenol (Figure 1B). We and others have shown that such synthetic phenol precursors, which have yet to undergo a Winstein Ar-3’ spirocyclization, are indistinguishable from their subsequent cyclized and biologically active cyclopropane containing counterparts in cell growth inhibition assays, DNA alkylation properties (rate, efficiency, and selectivity), and in vivo tumor models.7 Due to this indistinguishable behavior, protection of the seco-derivative phenol presents an attractive manner by which to prepare inactive prodrugs that can be cleaved in vivo with release of the active drug.6 Although prodrugs that use this protection and release strategy have been developed, surprisingly few to date incorporated features that allow selective tumor cell delivery or cleavage. Rather, most have been designed to permit rapid free drug release upon in vivo administration and typically incorporated features to permit their safe handling or improve drug physical properties (e.g., solubility). Beyond the most widely examined approach based on hydrolysis of an acylated phenol15–21 or phosphate prodrug,22 alternatives have been explored,23–25 including the use of masking functionality that can be reductively activated.26–35 Early examples of the reductively activated prodrugs include Denny’s nitro precursors to aryl amine variants of the phenol drugs,26–28 Lee’s use of an ester prodrug subject to cleavage upon a tethered quinone reduction,29 and our report of a mitomycin-like quinone precursor that undergoes an o-spirocyclization upon reductive activation.30 Recent examples have incorporated reducible peroxide31 or disulfide bonds32 to trigger free drug release. Prior to these latter studies, we introduced a unique set of N-acyl O-aminophenol prodrugs33–35 incorporated into the simpler, more stable, and more potent synthetic CBI alkylation subunit (Figure 1)36–39 for potential activation by N–O bond cleavage in the hypoxic environment of a solid tumor with its increased concentration of reducing nucleophiles. Cleavage of this previously unknown prodrug chemotype was projected to occur in a manner analogous to a disulfide bond, but with tunable control over the N–O bond cleavage reactivity. In these studies, a remarkable range of prodrug stabilities and propensity for N–O bond cleavage was observed even with subtle variations in the electronic and steric environment around the N–O bond.34 A subset of these prodrugs, including 1 and 2 (Figure 1B), exhibited outstanding stability in vitro and in vivo, displayed minimal or a lack of in vivo toxicity characteristic of this drug class (e.g., myelosuppression), provided an expanded tolerated dose range in vivo, and demonstrated superb efficacy against in vivo tumor models over those of the free drugs.33–35 These and related observations indicated that such N–O prodrugs afford advantages related to their preferential site, slow and sustained rate, and mechanism of free drug release. Herein, we report studies that provide insights into the reductive N–O bond cleavage and free drug release of N-acyl O-aminophenol duocarmycin prodrugs. Combined, the results of the studies are consistent with an exclusive intracellular protein-mediated (enantio)selective activation and free drug release from prodrug 1 by N–O bond cleavage preferentially in cancer cell lines versus cultured normal human cell lines effected by a cytosolic cysteine-based enzyme and suggest that the activating protein is one that is selectively expressed, upregulated, or preferentially activated in cancer cell lines potentially constituting a new oncology targeted precision therapy.

## Results and Discussion

### Relative Reactivities.

As reported elsewhere, the N–O bond stability and susceptibility to cleavage of a series of such cyclic and acyclic N–O prodrugs provided a full spectrum of reactivities.33–35 For example, compound 1 was found to be remarkably stable, being among the most stable of those examined and displaying little or no N–O bond cleavage in pH 7.6 phosphate buffer (t1/2 >4 weeks), human plasma (t1/2 >1 week, <5% free drug), and mouse plasma (t1/2 >48 h) at 25 °C.35 It proved robust toward acidic conditions, displaying a t1/2 >72 h in 4 N HCl/EtOAc and t1/2 = 30 h in 1:1 TFA/CH2Cl2, and stable in aqueous 0.1 N HCl (24 h, 97%).35 It was found to be stable toward aqueous 3% H2O2 (24 h, 100%), 0.1 N NaOH (24 h, 93%), and heat (105 °C, 7 d, 99.8%).35 Similarly, we found that incubation of 1 in cell culture media alone does not result in significant prodrug consumption, consistent with prodrug activation intracellularly when examined in cellular assays. Prodrug 2 was found to be more reactive but still unusually stable, displaying subtle distinctions from 1.33 Most relevant to a potential source of activation under physiological conditions, slow cleavage of prodrug 2 was observed in pH 7.6 phosphate buffer (20–40% after 72 h), and 2 was observed to exhibit a shorter half-life in human plasma (t1/2 = 3–6 h) at 25 °C with clean release of 3 and its subsequent spirocyclization to CBI-indole2 (4).33 Finally, prodrugs 1 or 2 did not alkylate DNA in cell free systems, indicating that activity observed in cell-based assays or in vivo tumor models requires cleavage of the prodrug N–O bond with release of free drug.33,35

### Cell Growth Inhibition Studies.

The cell growth inhibition activity of the prodrugs 1 and 2 in a representative panel of murine and human tumor cell lines was assessed alongside seco-CBI-indole2 (3) to identify those that may display hypersensitive or resistant tumor cell growth inhibition. Although 1–3 exhibit clearly differentiated in vitro potencies in cell growth inhibition assays (3 > 2 > 1) that mirror the N–O bond cleavage reactivities of 1 and 2, these studies did not identify a cell line that is either resistant or hypersensitive to 1 or 2 (Supporting Information Table S1). Even efforts to isolate resistant cell variants by serial, continuous, or metronomic exposure of sensitive cell lines (1: MDA-MB-231, BT549, and MMTV-PyMT human triple negative breast cancer) to sublethal concentrations of 1 over extended time periods failed to raise resistant or insensitive cancer cell populations. Although this did not provide an approach by which the source of prodrug activation could be identified, these observations suggest that the prodrug 1 and its mechanism of free drug release do not easily raise resistance and that 1 is not likely susceptible to common mechanisms of resistance, including Pgp efflux/transport of drug/prodrug or deactivating intracellular metabolism.

These studies were followed initially by conducting indirect functional cancer cell growth assays and later with a more informative cell lysate assay for direct measurement of free drug release. The later revealed the exclusive reliance on a specific protein-mediated mechanism of prodrug activation for 1, but not 2, without significant non-specific N–O bond cleavage. Initially, cancer cell growth inhibition studies were conducted in the presence of pan inhibitors of key enzyme classes, specific inhibitors of enzymes known to participate in the reductive activation of other (pro)drugs, and pharmacological tools used to probe other features potentially required for reductive activation.40 Consistent with the novel prodrug design, known mechanisms involved in reductive activation pathways did not appear to be operative, where cell growth inhibition was largely unaffected by the addition of pan inhibitors of the enzyme class or specific inhibitors of a potential candidate enzyme. These studies were conducted with a murine leukemia cell line (L1210) with an additional assessment often conducted with a human colon cancer cell line (HCT116). These studies first probed the participation of oxidoreductases and flavoreductases (diphenyleneiodonium chloride (DPI)41 pan inhibition, 1 μM) such as the nitroreductases42 and quinone reductases like DT-diaphorase (DTD, dicoumarol43 pan inhibition, 10 and 100 μM) without detection of an effect derived from inhibition of the protein classes most commonly involved in (prodrug) reductive activation.40b,c Similarly, the family of aldehyde dehydrogenases (ALDH) was an especially attractive candidate based on the work of others that have implicated it as a target of simplified duocarmyins.44 However, both pan inhibition of ALDH (gossypol45 at 100 nM, but a broadly promiscuous inhibitor) and more selective ALDH2/ALDH1A1 inhibition (disulfiram46 at 10 nM) were largely ineffective at blocking the cellular activity of the prodrug 1. Inhibitors of thioredoxin or glutathione reductase (PX-1247 at 1 μM and 2-AAPA48 at 2 μM), and glutathione S-transferases (GST, ethacrynic acid49,50 pan inhibition at 100 nM as well as specific GSTP1 inhibition with ezatiostat50 at 1 μM for G-site (glutathione site), and Las1751 at 1 μM for H-site (substrate site)) were also largely ineffective. All the above results above and those that follow below are summarized in Supporting Information Table S2. Even the addition of glutathione (1 mM) to the cell culture assay or depletion of intracellular glutathione levels with buthionine sulfoximine52 (BSO, 100 μM and 500 μM) as well as interference of NAD+ biosynthesis (FK866,53 10 nM) did not impact the functional cell growth inhibition activity of 1 and 2 (HCT116). Although not likely to be directly involved in the prodrug activation, pan inhibition of kinases (staurosporine, 5 μM), serine hydrolases/proteases (phenylmethysulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), 100 μM), and common proteases (protease inhibitor cocktail III), also did not impact the activity of the prodrug resulting from free drug release. However, most of the inhibitors or tool compounds examined and others considered display cytotoxic activity, limiting the concentrations that could be examined for an inhibitory effect on prodrug activation and conclusions that can be drawn from such studies. This limitation with the indirect functional cancer cell growth assays led to the development and use of a more informative cell lysate assay for direct measurement of prodrug consumption with its seco-derivative and free drug release.

### Additional Initial Studies.

Measurement of the in vitro enzymatic activities of two attractive enzyme candidates (glutathione S-transferases (GST), recombinant human glutathione S-transferase pi 1 (rhGSTP1), and recombinant human aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 A1 (rhALDH1A1)) were also conducted in initial studies and revealed that prodrug 1 remains largely unaffected by exposure to these enzymes as purified single entities. Pure rhALDH1A1 showed no significant inhibition in vitro in the presence of 1 (up to 10 μM) over a 24 h period (<5–7% inhibition) and no consumption of 1 with release of free drug was detected (Supporting Information Figure S1). Similarly, no global GST inhibition was observed following 1 h preincubation with prodrug 1 up to 10 μM concentration (Supporting Information Figure S2). Although 1 was capable of inhibiting GSTP1 in a more significant manner in an enzymatic assay, all CBI-indole2 analogs including 3, its inactive methyl ether, and 4 behaved similarly. When the enzymatic assay with pure rhGSTP1 was conducted in cell lysates (1 mg/mL protein, L1210), no GSTP1 inhibition by 1 was observed (Supporting Information Figure S3). Additionally, in situ inhibition of GSTP1 in HCT116 cells with Las17, an irreversible H-site (acceptor substrate) inhibitor, did not change the cell growth inhibition potency of 1 despite a measured reduction in the residual activity of GSTP1 (16% residual activity) (Supporting Information Figure S4). Finally, both short- and long-term depletion of cellular glutathione (GSH) with buthionine sulfoximine52 (BSO) in PC3-MM2 cells, with measured depletion of the intracellular concentration of the GSH, did not change the cell growth inhibition potency of 1 against the cell line (Supporting Information Figure S5 and Figure S6). Thus, although GSTP1 may bind 1 and related structures in vitro, it failed to do so in a detectable manner in cell lysates and its verified inhibition in situ with Las17 had no effect on the functional cell growth inhibition activity of 1, suggesting it is not directly involved in the activation of 1.

No evidence of either a serine hydrolase/protease or a cysteine-based enzyme interaction with 1 or 2 (1–10 μM) was detectable in activity-based protein profiling (ABPP)54 gel-based assays conducted with mouse brain, mouse liver, and both the soluble proteome and membrane-bound proteome of HCT116 cell lysates under conditions that measure either reversible55a or irreversible55b competitive active site binding, blocking the labeling of an enzyme by FP-Rh (serine hydrolase/protease), IA-Rh (cysteine hydrolase/protease, Supporting Information Figure S7) or AlexaFluor (lysine labeling). These studies established that members of the major enzyme classes (serine and cysteine hydrolase/proteases) or those that contain an active site lysine do not competitively sequester or covalently bind the prodrug/drug at a level that we could detect by ABPP probe labeling.

### Direct Prodrug Cleavage Assay and Initial Key Assessments in Cell Lysates.

These studies and others led to the development of a quantitative assay that directly measures conversion of prodrugs 1 and 2 to their N–O bond cleavage products in cell lysates. Cell lysates obtained by sonication in PBS buffer and normalized to 0.1 mg/mL protein (Lowry protein assay) were incubated at room temperature (30 min) followed by the addition of 1 or 2 in DMSO to achieve a 10 μM prodrug concentration (0.1% DMSO) and further incubated at 25 °C with duplicate sampling every 24 h (0, 24, 48, and 72 h) alongside a control 10 μM sample of prodrug in PBS buffer. At each time point, a 50 μL aliquot of the mixture was added to 200 μL of ethyl acetate containing an internal standard, vortexed, and 150 μL of the organic layer was removed and the solvent evaporated under a nitrogen stream. The residue was dissolved in 0.05% formic acid in acetonitrile and analyzed by LC-MS and LC-UV to quantitate the remaining 1 and metabolites relative to the internal standard (Figure 2). Because the relative amounts of both the released phenol (seco-derivative) and subsequent spirocyclized cyclopropane-containing free drug displayed variations resulting from ease of spirocyclization that is sensitive to processed sample handling following extraction from the cell lysates (i.e., storage time/conditions prior to sample analysis) whereas the prodrug 1 did not, the extent of prodrug consumption is reported in the series of studies that follow. In addition, we confirmed that prodrug cleavage with release of the seco-derivative and ultimately free drug is largely if not exclusively responsible for the observed prodrug consumption by lack of LC-MS detection of other potential metabolites. This included those derived from cleavage of the terminal indole (no M+H+ = m/z 447.10), cleavage release of the terminal indole2 carboxylic acid (no M+H+ = m/z 320.10 and/or 289.07), or glutathione (or related thiol) displacement of the chloride (no M+H+). Cell lysates from tumor cell lines (murine L1210 shown in Figure 2, and human HCT116) were used and quantitation of prodrug consumption versus an added internal standard was conducted by both mass spectrometry (MS, ion count) and UV upon LC separation of the cell lysate ethyl acetate extract. This assay was also used to demonstrate that consumption of 1 with release of seco and free drug occurs in the cell lysate and not PBS buffer, cell culture media, human plasma, or human serum, indicative of preferential intracellular versus extracellular prodrug activation that occurs at a slow and sustained rate (>72 h) (Supporting Information Figure S8). It was also used to examine the effect of added glutathione (GSH, 1000 μM) as a surrogate for free thiol reactivity in both PBS buffer and in L1210 cell lysates. No consumption of 1 was observed in PBS buffer (no effect, no prodrug cleavage or chloride displacement) in the presence of the added GSH (1000 μM) and interestingly resulted in a small reduction (not increase) in the amount of prodrug consumption in L1210 cell lysates (Supporting Information Figure S8).

In a key study, it was found that removal of proteins from the cell lysates by either membrane filtration (<3 kDa MWCO Amicon ultra spin filters, Figure 3) or acetonitrile precipitation, as well as simple protein inactivation by thermal denaturation (1% SDS, 96 °C, 15 min) prevents prodrug 1 consumption and free drug release, indicating that it is protein mediated (Figure 3, lysate – proteins). Additionally, it was found that removal of small molecules including free thiols such as glutathione from the cell lysates by dialysis or by using a desalting column (>7 kDa MWCO Zeba spin desalting resin column shown in Figure 3) while retaining protein content did not significantly inhibit prodrug 1 consumption and free drug release (Figure 3, lysate – small molecules). Because of the importance of this discovery and its implications on the mechanism of prodrug 1 activation, this assessment was repeated 20 times in duplicate (Figure 3, 40 assays with the two independent detection methods).

Separation of the soluble and membrane-bound proteome from L1210 lysed cells by ultracentrifugation indicated that the consumption of 1 with liberation of free drug occurs in the soluble proteome but not the membrane-bound proteome (Figure 4). A sequential detergent-based extraction of proteins from the subcellular fractions of the MCF-7 human breast cancer cell line without physical cell disruption was used to establish prodrug 1 consumption in the cytosolic, mitochondrial, and nuclear proteomes. The prodrug consumption with release of free drug was largely if not exclusively observed only in the cytosolic fraction (Figure 4) and the extent of prodrug consumption was nearly double that observed in unfractionated whole cell lysate when employing the same protein content (0.1 mg/mL), reflecting an enrichment in the activating protein.

The prodrug consumption was found to be greatest at pH 7.6 and diminished smoothly as the pH was raised or lowered from pH 7.6, as seen in experiments using L1210 cell lysates (Supporting Information Figure S8). Remarkably, only the natural enantiomer of 1 was found to be activated effectively in L1210 cell lysates whereas the unnatural enantiomer of 1 (ent-1) was not (Figure 5), consistent with a stereospecific protein-mediated reaction.

Finally, cell lysates from all murine and human cancer cell lines examined to date (>10 cell lines)56a were found to effectively consume 1 with release of free drug (Figure 6A) whereas cell lysates from cultured normal (non-transformed) cell lines examined to date56b (human astrocytes (AST), lung fibroblasts (HLF), dermal fibroblasts (HDF), neural progenitor cells (NPG), normal chondrocytes (NHAcs), and murine embryonic fibroblasts (NIH3T3)) do so far less effectively or fail to do so (Figure 6B).

Combined, these studies reveal that consumption of prodrug 1 with release of free drug through N–O bond cleavage is: (1) mediated by a protein found predominantly or exclusively in the cell cytosol, (2) preferentially occurs in cell lysates from murine or human cancer cell lines versus normal human or murine cell lines, and (3) proceeds at a slow rate over a sustained period of time (>72 h).

Finally, both 1 and 2 were found to display similar slow rates and overall efficiencies of prodrug activation in L1210 cell lysates but 1 displays a much greater and essentially complete stability in PBS buffer, cell culture media, human serum and human plasma, exhibiting little or no consumption after 72 h (Supporting Information Figure S8). This exclusive reliance on a protein-mediated mechanism of prodrug activation for 1, but not 2 (Supporting Information Figure S8), without significant non-specific N–O bond cleavage along with its preferential activation in cancer versus normal cell lines is likely the reason 1 exhibits a superior in vivo pharmacological safety profile, further improved efficacy, and larger therapeutic window than 2.

### Characterization of the Cleavage Protein in Cell Lysates with Chemical Probe and Enzyme Inhibitor Assessments.

To better understand the nature of the protein(s) responsible for the prodrug cleavage with free drug release and to complement the functional cell-based assays and overcome its limitations, the direct prodrug cleavage assay in cell lysates (L1210 lysates) was used to survey candidate enzyme and protein classes. Summarized in Figure 7A are the results of an initial study and structures of all enzyme inhibitors and the chemical probes examined for concentration-dependent blockage of the prodrug consumption are shown in Figure 7B. Plotted data for the ineffective inhibitors is provided in Supporting Information Figure S10. Notably, the assessment in lysates permitted a much larger range of inhibitor concentrations to be examined for an effect and was typically conducted at range starting at 10 or 1 mM down to as low as 0.1 μM.

Consistent with observations made in the cell-based assays, L1210 cell lysates treated with diphenyleneiodonium chloride (DPI),41,42 a pan inhibitor of the oxidoreductases/flavoreductases including the nitroreductases, as well as dicoumarol,43 a pan inhibitor of quinone reductases (e.g., DT-diaphorase), had little impact on the prodrug consumption (Supporting Information Figure S10). Similarly, pan inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenases44 was also largely ineffective (gossypol,45 Supporting Information Figure S11). Concurrent with these studies and because the family of aldehyde dehydrogenases (ALDH) was an especially attractive candidate based on the work of others,44 particularly ALDH1A1, the inhibitors disulfiram46 for more specific ALDH2/ALDH1A1 inhibition and CM3760 for specific inhibition of ALDH1A1 were also examined (Figure S11). Both disulfiram and CM37 failed to block the L1210 lysate consumption of 1 at concentrations up to 1 mM, the highest concentration examined.

L1210 cell lysates treated with the pan serine hydrolase inhibitor phenylmethysulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) as well as pan inhibition of the kinases (staurosporine),57 protein phosphatases (cantharidin and cantharidic acid),58 and HDACs (SAHA)59 failed to block prodrug consumption in the L1210 lysate (Supporting Information Figure S10). The latter rather nonselective inhibitor, being a hydroxamic acid that chelates protein bound zinc, might also suggest other members of the zinc metalloenzyme superfamily may not be involved in the activation of 1. The metal chelating compound EDTA displayed only a weak concentration dependent inhibition at 1–10 mM and no inhibition at and below 100 μM (Supporting Information Figure S10). Although this might rule out an integral role of a metal ion since 1–5 mM EDTA is recommended for inhibiting metalloproteases in cell lysates, we are uncertain how to accurately interpret this result and cannot exclude its action on a metalloenzyme. Similarly, the metal chelation compound 1,10-phenanthroline exhibited weak and incomplete inhibition of cell lysate prodrug 1 consumption at 10–0.1 mM and no inhibition at lower concentrations. These results and those for all ineffective inhibitors discussed above are provided in Supporting Information Figure S10. The observations made in the studies above were overshadowed by the behavior of pan cysteine-reactive chemical probes (e.g., 2-iodoacetamide) and with a host of additional inhibitors of proteins that rely on cysteine-based functional activity, including ebselen61 that bears a striking structural similarity to the prodrug 1 active moiety (Figure 8).

Despite the reactivity of 2-iodoacetamide, it displayed a surprisingly smooth dose-dependent and time-dependent inhibition of lysate prodrug consumption. The more potent blockage of prodrug consumption by ebselen was complete at 1 mM and 100 μM and dose-dependent inhibition was observed at lower concentrations with activity even observable at 0.1 μM (lowest concentration tested). The action of ebselen, a promiscuous inhibitor,61,62 likely entails cysteine thiol nucleophilic attack at selenium with cleavage of the reactive Se–NPh bond to form a protein covalent adduct. Subsequent cleavage of the fragile Se–S bond by intermolecular nucleophilic attack then releases reduced ebselen. In the case of proteins with two proximal cysteines, a second intramolecular cysteine thiol nucleophilic cleavage of the bound weak Se–S bond could release reduced ebselen and the oxidized protein disulfide (Figure 8). Additional effective cysteine reactive electrophiles are discussed below and were also found to block prodrug consumption in a similar well-defined concentration-dependent manner, further supporting a protein-embedded cysteine participation in the prodrug cleavage and activation.

Finally, the effect of lysine acylation was examined with the widely used 4-phenylbutanoate-NHS ester probe, which displayed a modest concentration-dependent blockage of prodrug consumption (Supporting Information Figure S13). This is listed in Figure 7A in a category entitled lysine containing proteins. However, while this probe is widely used for effective active site lysine acylation in proteins, it is modestly reactive toward both active site serine and cysteine. Consequently, it is presently unclear whether this result indicates weak blockage through inefficient reaction with a lysine directly involved in prodrug consumption, a lysine proximal to a protein reaction site, or whether it is the result of the relatively inefficient acylation of a participating active site cysteine/serine.

Combined, these results are consistent with N–O bond cleavage and free drug release by a cysteine-based enzyme/protein located in the cell cytosol. Consequently, studies were conducted with additional cysteine reactive enzyme inhibitors and chemical probes to further confirm cysteine participation in the prodrug activation. As highlighted in the discussions of their use, some are broadly reactive toward cysteine and some are known to act on subsets of attractive candidate enzymes or protein classes, including reductases bearing proximal cysteines capable of both cleavage and release of the prodrug. The most potent of these was conoidin A,63 reported as a covalent pan inhibitor of the peroxiredoxins, that cross-links proximal active site cysteines (reactive reducing cysteine and resolving oxidation cysteine) but with promiscuous behavior toward many other enzymes.63 Like ebselen, it displayed full inhibition of the consumption of prodrug 1 at 1 mM and 100 μM, a well-defined concentration-dependent inhibition throughout the lower concentration range, and activity even at 0.1 μM (Figure 9). Similarly, celastrol,64 a recently disclosed and putatively more selective covalent pan inhibitor of the peroxiredoxins targeting cysteine, displayed full blockage at 1 mM and 100 μM, a similarly well-defined concentration-dependent inhibition of the prodrug consumption at the lower concentrations, and activity at 1 μM or perhaps even lower (Figure 9).

An especially attractive candidate enzyme class for prodrug 1 activation because of the proximal reactive and resolving cysteines in the active site as well as its use in activating duocarmycin prodrugs through a tethered disulfide cleavage reaction,32 is thioredoxin. A competitive and slow irreversible inhibitor of thioredoxin-1 (PX-1247) that targets cysteine did not display effective blockage of prodrug consumption, exhibiting modest activity only at the highest concentration examined (1 mM) (Supporting Information Figure S15). However, the inhibitor AAPA,48 which has been shown to inhibit both thioredoxin reductase (TrxR), which also bears an active site reactive cysteine/selenocysteine and a resolving cysteine, as well as glutathione reductase (GR), displayed potent concentration-dependent blockage of the lysate consumption of prodrug 1 (Supporting Information Figure S15). Notably, AAPA (2 μM) did not impact the cellular in vitro cytotoxic activity of 1 against L1210 but higher concentrations could not be examined because of the cytotoxic activity of AAPA itself.65

Interestingly, the respectively selective cysteine-targeting irreversible inhibitor RSL3 (1 h preincubation in lysates),66 first reported as putative inhibitor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and later established to be a TxnR-D1 inhibitor,66b also displayed effective concentration-dependent blockade of the L1210 lysate consumption of prodrug 1 (Figure 9), albeit not as potently as ebselen or conoidin A. GPX4 is a protein in which a selenocysteine versus cysteine is the active site nucleophilic residue responsible for reaction with and reduction of H2O2 and lipid peroxides released upon oxidative stress. Notably, we do not wish to imply GPX4 may be involved in the prodrug activation because of the action of RSL3. In fact, removal of small molecules, including glutathione required for reduced GPX4 regeneration, did not impact L1210 lysate consumption of 1 (Figure 3), depletion of glutathione with BSO did not impact cell growth inhibition by 1 (HCT116 and PC3-MM2 (Supporting Information Figures S5 and S6), and addition of glutathione (1000 μM) to the L1210 lysate assay did not enhance prodrug consumption (Supporting Information Figure S8). Rather, these studies would seem to suggest GPX4 is not the protein involved in activation of 1.

Not all thiol reactive enzyme inhibitors or probes interfere with lysate-mediated prodrug 1 consumption. Two putatively selective inhibitors of deubiquitinases (DUBs), degrasyn67 (WP1130, inhibits UCHL5 as well as USP5, UCHL1, USP9x and USP14) and b-AP1568 (inhibits USP14 and UCHL5, two 19S protesome DUBs), did not effectively block prodrug 1 consumption in L1210 cell lysates at reasonable concentrations (no or little inhibition at ≤100 μM, (Supporting Information Figure S10). It is notable that despite the promiscuous activity of such electrophilic Michael-acceptor inhibitors toward protein-embedded cysteines69 that provide covalently bound adducts, this inhibitor class does not seem to be especially effective at targeting the protein(s) responsible for the activation of prodrug 1. Further representative of this generalization, ethacrynic acid49 was also not effective at blocking the action of L1210 cell lysates on prodrug 1 (no or little inhibition at ≤100 μM, Supporting Information Figure S10). Ethacrynic acid (edecrin) as well as its glutathione adduct are reversible covalent pan inhibitors of glutathione S-transferases (GST). This result reinforces others presented herein suggesting that GSTs are not the protein class responsible for activation of prodrug 1. Surprisingly, the promiscuous inhibitor auranofin50 was also largely ineffective at blocking the L1210 lysate consumption of 1, displaying no blockage at concentrations of 100 μM and lower and only partial blockage at 1 mM (Supporting Information Figure S10). Auranofin inhibits numerous reduction/oxidation enzymes, including thioredoxin reductase (TrxR) where it has been most studied. Auranofin has a high affinity for thiol and selenol groups, to which it forms stable irreversible adducts. It also inhibits glutathione S-transferases, binding at the H-site (substrate site), as well as the 19S proteasome-associated deubiquitinases (DUBs).50

E-64, an epoxide that irreversibly inhibits a range of cysteine peptidases including papain, cathepsin B, cathepsin L, calpain and staphopain, did not effectively block prodrug consumption in the L1210 cell lysates at reasonable concentrations (Supporting Information Figure S10). This observation suggests that this inhibitor class may not effectively target the prodrug cleaving protein and potentially that such cysteine proteases may not be involved.

Finally, and as a cautionary note, the studies above do not establish that the activating reactive cysteine is directly involved in enzyme catalysis. Flufenamic acid also exhibited a modest dose-dependent inhibition of prodrug 1 consumption (Supporting information Figure S16). Among its properties, it is an inhibitor of aldo-keto reductases (AKRs)70 that catalyze redox transformations involved in biosynthesis, intermediary metabolism and detoxification. They are enzymes that do not contain catalytic active site cysteines. However, a unique feature of AKR1B1 (and perhaps other family members) is its sensitivity to oxidation. A hyper-reactive cysteine residue is located at the AKR1B1 active site and its oxidation accelerates catalysis and prevents inhibitor binding.71 Several studies have suggested that oxidation of this cysteine is a physiological process and represents an important mode of redox enzyme regulation.

Combined, the use of chemical probes and enzyme inhibitors that target classes of proteins in the cell lysate (L1210) assay indicate the protein located in the cell cytosol responsible for N–O bond cleavage with free drug release likely contains a reactive cysteine (or selenocysteine) and suggest that many of the common mechanisms of reductive activation characterized to date are not operative with 1.

## Conclusions

Herein, we detail studies that provide insights into the mechanism of free drug release for a unique class of N-acyl O-aminophenol prodrugs that map seamlessly onto the core structure of duocarmycin analogues.72 With use of a direct assay for prodrug cleavage in cell lysates, the results of the combined studies are consistent with a slow and sustained stereoselective activation and free drug release (>72 h) from prodrug 1 by N–O bond cleavage effected by a cysteine-based (or selenocysteine-based) enzyme/protein located in the cell cytosol preferentially in cancer cell lines, likely constituting a new oncology targeted precision therapy. This exclusive reliance on an intracellular protein-mediated mechanism of prodrug activation for 1, but not 2, without significant non-specific N–O bond cleavage along with its preferential free drug release in cancer versus normal cell lines is likely the reason 1 exhibits a superior in vivo pharmacological safety profile, further improved in vivo efficacy, and larger therapeutic window than 2. Although the intrinsic selectivity of many of the inhibitors and probes used to characterize the protein-mediated mechanism of activation is low to modest, an interesting observation that emerged from the studies is the potential that the activating protein may be a member of an enzyme family containing proximal reactive and resolving cysteines at the active site. Given the efficacious in vivo antitumor activity of 1 and its lack of toxicity characteristic of traditional chemotherapeutic drugs, the protein responsible for its activation is also likely one that is selectively expressed, upregulated, or uniquely activated in cancer cell lines, effectively taming the nonselective exceptional potency of the free drug and targeting its release.
